pl: Capernaum, north shore of the Sea of Galilee
per: 1st century AD, with a church built over it in the 5th
w: Franciscan archaeologists (from 1968) dug under an octagonal church and found a cluster of small basalt houses around shared courtyards. One room was plastered and used for gatherings from the 1st century on, and later got a church of its own.
m: The Gospels place Jesus’ base, and Simon Peter’s home, in Capernaum. The early veneration of this one house, and the way it changed from a home into a meeting place, makes it a strong candidate.
c: No inscription names Peter. The link rests on early veneration, not on a signed doorway.
r: Mark 1:29-31; Mark 2:1-12; Matthew 8:14-17; Luke 4:38-41; Matthew 9:1-8; Mark 3:20-21

n: Capernaum: the white synagogue and the black one beneath
per: White building 4th–5th century AD; basalt foundations below are earlier
w: The striking white limestone synagogue visible today is later than Jesus. Beneath it, excavators found black basalt walls and a pavement that many think belonged to a 1st-century synagogue.
m: Luke says a Roman centurion helped build the town’s synagogue, and Mark and Luke show Jesus teaching and healing there on the Sabbath. The basalt layer is the likeliest remnant of that building.
c: The white building you see is 300+ years after Jesus; scholars still argue about its exact date and about the basalt layer.

w: In the drought of 1986 two brothers spotted the outline of a wooden hull in the exposed mud. It is about 27 ft (8.2 m) long and 7.5 ft (2.3 m) wide, patched with at least a dozen kinds of wood, and could hold around 15 people. Radiocarbon and pottery date it to Jesus’ time.
m: It shows the kind of working fishing boat the Gospels describe: a vessel big enough to carry a teacher and a few disciples, to be rowed or sailed across the lake, or to serve as a floating platform near the shore.
c: The nickname is modern. Nothing links this boat to Jesus or his disciples; it is evidence of the same world.

n: Fishing on the lake: hooks, weights and salted fish
w: Lead weights for casting nets, stone anchors and bronze fishhooks turn up at lakeshore sites such as Magdala and Bethsaida. Magdala’s Greek name, Taricheae, means “salted fish”, and it was a processing center for the catch.
m: It was a real trade with owners, hired men and partners, as Zebedee and his sons show. Fishing also fed the economy that taxes and tolls were collected from along the shore.

n: Magdala: a synagogue with a carved stone
pl: Magdala (Migdal), west shore of the lake
per: 1st century BC – AD 67 (the town was destroyed in the revolt)
w: Excavations since 2009 uncovered a 1st-century synagogue, a market, harbor installations and ritual baths. In the synagogue hall lay the Magdala Stone, carved with a seven-branched menorah and other Temple symbols.
m: Magdala was the home of Mary Magdalene. The synagogue is one of the very few from Jesus’ lifetime, and the stone suggests how closely Galilean Jews felt tied to the Jerusalem Temple.
c: The Gospels never say Jesus taught in Magdala’s synagogue; it shows the setting, not a recorded event.
r: Luke 8:1-3; Mark 15:40-41; Mark 16:1-8; John 20:1-18; Matthew 15:39; Matthew 16:1-4; Mark 8:10

per: Mosaic about AD 450–480 (church tradition from the 4th century)
w: A Byzantine church floor in front of the altar shows a basket of loaves flanked by two fish. Nearby springs flowed into the lake, the “seven springs” (Heptapegon) that gave the place its Arabic name.
m: Pilgrims since the 4th century have remembered the feeding of the crowd here, and the nearby shoreline chapel recalls the breakfast on the beach after the resurrection.
c: The Gospels do not name the exact spot, and John places the feeding near Bethsaida; Tabgha is the traditional site.

n: Chorazin: a town of black basalt
per: Town of Jesus’ day; ornate synagogue 3rd–4th century AD
w: Excavations show a basalt town with houses, olive presses and ritual baths. Its later synagogue is richly carved and held a basalt “Seat of Moses” for the one reading the Law.
m: Jesus names Chorazin with Bethsaida and Capernaum as towns that saw his miracles and did not repent, yet the Gospels record none of those miracles. The town shows how much of his work we do not read about.
c: The impressive synagogue is later than Jesus, though a 1st-century settlement lay beneath it.

n: Bethsaida: et-Tell and a rival site
pl: North shore of the lake, east of the Jordan
per: 1st century AD (city of Philip the tetrarch)
w: At et-Tell, excavators found an Iron Age city gate, and Hellenistic and Roman houses, including a so-called fisherman’s house with hooks and net weights. A second candidate, el-Araj, nearer the shore, has been dug since 2015.
m: Bethsaida was the hometown of Peter, Andrew and Philip, and the place where Jesus healed a blind man by stages and (by Luke) fed the five thousand nearby.
c: Which mound is the true Bethsaida is still debated.

per: Shrine of Pan from the 3rd century BC; Philip’s city from 2 BC
w: A large cave and a strong spring pour out at the foot of Mount Hermon. Beside them are niches carved for the god Pan and the nymphs, and the footings of a temple Herod built for Augustus. Philip the tetrarch renamed the city Caesarea.
m: Jesus asks his disciples “Who do people say that I am?” in the district around this pagan city. Some scholars suggest the cave, regarded as a gate to the underworld, forms the backdrop for “the gates of Hades.”
c: The Gospels never describe the shrine; the connection to “gates of Hades” is a suggestion, not a statement.

n: The east shore: Kursi, Gadara and Hippos
pl: Sea of Galilee’s east shore and the Decapolis
per: Roman Decapolis cities; Byzantine monastery at Kursi
w: Kursi, on the steep eastern shore, has a large Byzantine monastery and church that, by tradition, mark the healing of the demoniac. Gadara (Umm Qais) kept a theater and colonnaded street, and Hippos (Sussita) a hilltop forum and church.
m: This was Gentile country, the Decapolis, where pigs were raised. Matthew, Mark and Luke use different names for the district (Gadarenes, Gerasenes), which tells us the story’s location was already being remembered in several ways.
c: Kursi is the traditional site only; Gadara and Gerasa are inland, and the Gospels’ own names differ.

n: Tiberias and Sepphoris: Herod Antipas’s new cities
per: Sepphoris rebuilt after 4 BC; Tiberias founded AD 18–20
w: Antipas rebuilt Sepphoris, about 6 km (under 4 miles) from Nazareth, as a showpiece capital with a theater, and founded Tiberias on the lake. Excavations show Roman-style streets, public baths and prosperous houses.
m: Jesus grew up between these projects. The Gospels never say he entered either city, though the lake bears the name “Sea of Tiberias” in John, and Antipas, the city’s founder, appears in the story of John the Baptist.
c: The Gospels do not mention a visit to either city; the possibility that Jesus worked there as a builder is a scholar’s guess.
r: John 6:1; John 6:23; John 21:1; Mark 6:14-29; Luke 13:31-33; Mark 6:3

per: Village of the 1st century BC – 1st century AD
w: Digs under and around modern Nazareth reveal a small farming village: cisterns, grain silos, wine and olive presses and rock-cut tombs. A 1st-century house was found beside the Church of the Annunciation, and “Nazareth Village” is a modern reconstruction on an excavated farm.
m: This is the setting of Jesus’ childhood and the synagogue scene in Luke 4. The finds confirm a modest place with a few dozen households, matching Nathanael’s question, “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?”
c: Nazareth Village is a reconstruction, and the grotto under the Church of the Annunciation is venerated, not proved.
r: Luke 1:26-38; Luke 2:39-40; Luke 4:16-30; Matthew 2:23; John 1:45-46; Matthew 13:53-58

w: Khirbet Qana, a ruin about 14 km north of Nazareth, has Roman-era houses, tombs, and later pilgrim sites. Kafr Kanna, the modern village nearer to Nazareth, hosts the traditional Wedding Church.
m: Two signs happen at Cana in John’s Gospel: the water into wine and the healing of an official’s son. Which village it was affects the route Jesus took.
c: Some scholars prefer Khirbet Qana (older name, early pilgrim reports); Kafr Kanna has the longer pilgrim tradition. No inscription settles it.

per: Fortified in the 1st century; churches from the 4th–6th centuries
w: A rounded mountain rising out of the Jezreel Valley, crowned by a Franciscan basilica (1924) and a Greek Orthodox church. Josephus says he fortified the summit in AD 66, so it was a military site in the lifetime of the first Christians.
m: Christians from the 4th century on have honored Tabor as the mountain of the Transfiguration, though the Gospels simply say “a high mountain”.
c: An alternate site is Mount Hermon, nearer to Caesarea Philippi. The Gospels give no name.

per: Church built 1938; tradition from the 4th century
w: A hill above the lake with a small octagonal church (1938) and a broad natural slope that works like an amphitheater. The pilgrim Egeria in the 4th century mentions a cave and a hillside nearby that were honored in memory of the sermon.
m: Matthew places Jesus’ great sermon “on the mountain”; Luke says “on a level place.” Neither names the spot, but the lakeshore slopes make it easy to see how a large crowd could hear one voice.
c: The site is traditional. The Gospels don’t say where the sermon was given.

n: Synagogues of Jesus’ day: Gamla, Magdala and the Theodotus stone
w: Gamla, a town on the Golan destroyed by Rome in AD 67, preserved a basalt synagogue with stone benches around the walls. In Jerusalem, a Greek inscription (the Theodotus stone) records a synagogue built “for the reading of the Law and the teaching of the commandments,” with a guesthouse for travelers.
m: The Gospels picture Jesus reading and teaching in synagogues. These buildings show they were community halls as much as places of worship: meeting rooms, schools and hostels.
c: Few synagogues from before AD 70 survive, so scholars debate exactly how they were used.
r: Luke 4:16-21; Mark 1:21; Mark 6:1-6; Matthew 4:23; John 18:20; Luke 13:10-17; Mark 5:22; Matthew 9:35; Matthew 10:17; Matthew 12:9-14; Mark 3:1-6

n: Qumran and the Dead Sea Scrolls
pl: Northwest shore of the Dead Sea
per: Settlement 2nd century BC – AD 68; scrolls about 250 BC – AD 68
w: Between 1947 and 1956 shepherds and archaeologists found hundreds of scrolls in eleven caves above a desert settlement. The settlement has stepped, plastered pools used for ritual washing and a long communal dining room.
m: The community saw itself as the voice “crying in the wilderness” of Isaiah 40:3, the same verse the Gospels apply to John the Baptist. It shows that waiting for God’s coming in the Judean desert and ritual immersion were part of Jewish life in Jesus’ day.
c: There is no evidence that John or Jesus visited Qumran. The scrolls are background, not a record of the Gospel events.

pl: Found in Qumran Cave 1; kept at the Israel Museum, Jerusalem
w: A nearly complete scroll of Isaiah, about 7.3 m (24 ft) long, sewn from 17 sheets of parchment. It was found in 1947 and is the oldest copy of the whole book of Isaiah by over a thousand years.
m: In the Nazareth synagogue Jesus is handed the scroll of Isaiah and finds the passage about the Lord’s anointed. This is what such a scroll looked like and how it was unrolled.
c: It is a Dead Sea scroll, not the one Jesus held, but a copy of the same text from his world.
r: Luke 4:16-21; Matthew 3:3; Mark 1:2-3; Luke 3:4-6; John 12:38-41; Luke 7:22

n: Al-Maghtas and Qasr al-Yahud: where John baptized
pl: Lower Jordan River, east and west banks
per: Byzantine churches 5th–6th century; tradition from the 4th century
w: On the east bank (Jordan), a UNESCO site has pools, baptism steps and several churches, with “Elijah’s Hill” nearby. On the west bank, across the river, Qasr al-Yahud has its own monasteries. Pilgrims from the 4th century, and the 6th-century Madaba mosaic map, mark this stretch.
m: John 1:28 says John baptized at “Bethany beyond the Jordan,” which fits the east bank. The two sites stand opposite each other.
c: Both banks honor the baptism; no inscription names the spot.

per: Hermits from the 4th century; Orthodox monastery 1895
w: A steep desert cliff above Jericho with caves where hermits lived from the early Byzantine period. A Greek Orthodox monastery clings to the rock face.
m: Christians have long linked this wilderness to the forty days Jesus fasted. The name Quarantal comes from the Latin for “forty”.
c: The Gospels say only “the wilderness”. The identification is traditional.

per: Rebuilt by Herod the Great, in use in Jesus’ day
w: A fortress-palace on a lonely ridge, with a bath, a dining hall and cells cut in the rock. Italian and Hungarian digs have exposed its rooms and the Roman siege ramp from AD 72.
m: The Jewish historian Josephus says John the Baptist was imprisoned and killed here by Herod Antipas. The Gospels give the banquet and the beheading but never name the place.
c: The location comes from Josephus, not the Gospels.

n: Herodium: the fortress-palace of Herod the Great
w: An artificial cone-shaped hill with a circular palace, a theater with a royal box and, in 2007, the discovery of what its excavator, Ehud Netzer, believed was Herod’s tomb. Floors with mosaics and wall plaster survive in the palace.
m: Herod’s paranoid rule frames the birth narrative: Matthew pictures him searching for the child king. The Herodium shows the wealth and defensive mindset of the ruler who died here in 4 BC (his burial there is described by Josephus).
c: The Gospels never mention Herodium; it illustrates the world around the story.

n: Jericho: three cities in one valley
per: Herod’s palaces 1st century BC–AD 1; Old Testament Jericho thousands of years earlier
w: Tell es-Sultan, Old Testament Jericho, is among the oldest cities known. The New Testament city lay a mile or two south, where Hasmonean and Herodian kings built winter palaces with pools, gardens and diamond-patterned stonework. Herod died here in 4 BC.
m: Jesus passes through the oasis on his last journey up to Jerusalem, healing blind Bartimaeus on the way out and dining with Zacchaeus the chief tax collector, a man whose wealth fits the toll-rich palace town.
c: The Gospels’ Jericho is the Herodian oasis, not the mound of Joshua.

pl: Wadi Qelt and the desert descent
w: About 27 km (17 miles) of road drops from Jerusalem at roughly 750 m above sea level to Jericho more than 250 m below it. Parts of the Roman road, milestones and a ruined inn (Khan al-Hatrura, later Ottoman) survive in the Wadi Qelt.
m: The Good Samaritan is set on this road: steep, remote, ideal for ambush. Jesus’ audience would have known exactly how dangerous it was.
c: The “Inn of the Good Samaritan” is a later building on the traditional site; the parable is a story, not a place report.

n: The Church of the Nativity, Bethlehem
per: Built about AD 327–339; rebuilt in the 6th century
w: Constantine’s basilica was built over a cave honored as the birthplace, then rebuilt in the 6th century. In 1934 excavators uncovered a beautiful mosaic floor under the nave from the original church. Justin Martyr, around AD 160, already speaks of a cave in Bethlehem.
m: Luke 2 and Matthew 2 place Jesus’ birth in Bethlehem. The unbroken veneration of this one cave from the 2nd century is among the oldest Christian site traditions.
c: The Gospels do not mention a cave; some homes then used caves for animals, which is how the tradition took shape.

per: Byzantine monastery remains; folds in use since antiquity
w: East of Bethlehem, Byzantine ruins and cave-chapels mark the traditional field of the shepherds. Across the Judean hills, low stone walls and rock-cut enclosures are still used as night folds for sheep.
m: Luke has shepherds first to hear the birth; Jesus later calls himself the good shepherd who knows his sheep, enters through the gate and lays down his life.
c: Several villages claim the shepherds’ field. The Gospel does not locate it.

n: Old Cairo: the Holy Family’s tradition
per: Roman fortress of Babylon (2nd–4th century); church traditions from the 5th century on
w: In the district of Old Cairo, a Roman fortress called Babylon still has a surviving tower. Coptic churches, including the Church of St. Sergius, stand over a crypt traditionally said to be where the Holy Family sheltered.
m: Matthew says Joseph took Mary and the child to Egypt to flee Herod. Egypt had a large Jewish community, centered on Alexandria, so refuge there made sense.
c: The Gospel names no place in Egypt. The fortress itself is later than Jesus’ day.

per: Byzantine and Crusader churches; modern churches from 1885 and 1955
w: A village in the hills with two churches: the Church of the Visitation (1955) and St. John the Baptist, built on Byzantine and Crusader remains, marking where Elizabeth and Zechariah lived.
m: Luke says Mary travelled “into the hill country of Judea” to visit Elizabeth. The village has been honored as their home since the Byzantine centuries.
c: Luke names no village. Ein Karem’s link is traditional.

n: The Tel Dan Stele: the “House of David”
w: In 1993–94 archaeologists found fragments of an Aramaic victory inscription carved into basalt. One line names the “House of David” and the “king of Israel”. It is the earliest known reference to David’s dynasty outside the Bible.
m: Matthew opens with “the son of David” and Luke ties Jesus’ birth to David’s town. The stele shows that David’s dynasty was known to Israel’s neighbors centuries before Jesus.
c: The text is fragmentary, and scholars still debate its wording and which king wrote it.

n: The Temple Mount and the Western Wall
per: Herod’s rebuilding began about 20–19 BC; destroyed AD 70
w: Herod doubled the size of the platform to about 36 acres (14.4 hectares), faced it with enormous cut stones (some 13 m long, hundreds of tons), and added stairways, shops and gates. The lower courses of the Western Wall are Herod’s work. Broad stairs rise to the sealed Huldah Gates on the south.
m: This is the temple Jesus entered, taught in and predicted would fall. John records that it had been under construction for “forty-six years”, a timeline that fits Herod’s building campaign.
c: Nothing of the temple building itself survives; what remains is the platform around it.

pl: South-west corner of the Temple Mount
w: At the foot of the Western Wall, archaeologists found Herodian paving covered by massive stones hurled down by Roman soldiers in AD 70. One fallen block, carved “to the place of trumpeting”, once marked a spot where a priest sounded the Sabbath trumpet.
m: Jesus told his disciples that not one stone would be left on another. The rubble lies exactly as it fell, still on the street where Jesus’ contemporaries once walked.

w: A limestone block carved in Greek warns any foreigner not to pass beyond the barrier around the inner courts on penalty of death. It was found in 1871, and a second fragment was found in 1935. The first is in Istanbul, the second in Jerusalem.
m: The Jewish historian Josephus described this stone barrier. Jesus drove the traders out of the outer court, the Court of the Gentiles, the only part non-Jews could enter.

n: The Tyrian shekel and the Temple tax
w: The Temple tax had to be paid in Tyrian silver (a heavy, pure coin stamped with Melqart and an eagle). Money changers set up in the Temple courts to exchange common currency for it, and thousands of these coins turn up in Jerusalem.
m: This explains the money changers whose tables Jesus overturned, and the “shekel” Peter finds in the fish’s mouth to pay the tax for both of them.

w: Tiny bronze coins, weighing a gram or two, were minted by the Hasmonean kings and found in huge numbers in Judea. In Greek they are lepta, “thin ones”; Mark says two of them make a quadrans, the smallest Roman coin.
m: The poor widow dropped in two lepta, perhaps the smallest coins in circulation, and Jesus said she gave more than all the rich donors.

n: The denarius: the tribute penny and the day’s wage
w: The silver denarius of Tiberius shows the emperor’s head with the words “Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus”. It was the coin of a soldier’s pay and a laborer’s day. Greek silver drachmas were roughly equal in value.
m: When opponents asked about paying taxes to Caesar, Jesus asked for a coin and “whose image and inscription is this?” The same coin is the “denarius” of the workers in the vineyard and the lost drachma in Luke 15.
r: Mark 12:13-17; Matthew 22:15-22; Luke 20:20-26; Matthew 20:1-16; Luke 15:8-10; Matthew 18:21-35; Matthew 25:14-30

n: The Pilate Stone and Pilate’s coins
w: In 1961, Italian archaeologists at Caesarea’s theater found a carved block with a Latin dedication naming “Pontius Pilatus, prefect of Judea”. It is the only inscription from his lifetime naming him. Bronze coins he issued with pagan cult symbols still turn up.
m: It confirms Pilate as a real governor, with the title prefect, and Caesarea as the Roman capital where he lived. The Gospels move him between Caesarea and Jerusalem at Passover.
c: The original is in the Israel Museum; Caesarea displays a copy.

w: In 1990 construction work uncovered a burial cave with twelve ossuaries. Two bear the name “Joseph son of Caiaphas” and one, richly decorated, held the bones of a man of about sixty.
m: Josephus calls the high priest “Joseph, who was called Caiaphas”. If this is his tomb, it is the closest we get to the man who presided over the interrogation of Jesus.
c: Most scholars accept the identification, but some doubt it.

n: St Peter in Gallicantu and the high priest’s house
per: Church from 1931; site tradition from the 5th century
w: A church on the slope of Mount Zion stands over rock-cut rooms, cisterns and a pit-like prison cell. Nearby is an ancient stepped street, often dated to the 1st century, linking the lower city to Mount Zion.
m: Pilgrims from the Byzantine period honored this as the house of Caiaphas, where Jesus was questioned and Peter denied him before the rooster crowed.
c: The wealthy mansions excavated in the Upper City are better candidates for a high priest’s house. This one is a tradition.

n: The mansions of the Upper City and the Burnt House
w: Digs in the Upper City found grand houses with mosaics, painted plaster, stone tables, ritual baths and private courtyards. In the “Burnt House”, charred wood, a spear and a weight inscribed “of Bar Kathros” show the fire of AD 70.
m: This is where the priestly families lived. John describes the high priest’s courtyard, a fire in it, a doorkeeper and Peter warming his hands, details that fit a mansion of this kind.
r: John 18:15-18; Mark 14:54; Luke 22:55; Matthew 24:1-2; Matthew 19:21-24; Luke 16:19-31

w: In 2004, while repairing a sewer pipe, workers uncovered a large stepped pool with three tiers of stairs. Coins and pottery date it to the Second Temple period. It was fed by Hezekiah’s Tunnel.
m: In John 9 Jesus sends a blind man to wash in the pool, and John adds the meaning of its name (“Sent”). It was also the starting point of the water ceremony in the feast of Tabernacles that frames John 7.
c: A later Byzantine pool, further downstream, was long mistaken for the one in John.

pl: Jerusalem, from the Gihon Spring to Siloam
w: A water tunnel, 533 m (1,750 ft) long, cut through solid rock from the Gihon Spring to the Pool of Siloam. An inscription found in the tunnel, in ancient Hebrew, records the moment the two teams dug toward each other and met. You can still wade through it.
m: The tunnel brought water to the Pool of Siloam, the pool where Jesus sent the blind man, and it supplied the water used at Tabernacles.
c: The tunnel is 700 years older than Jesus. It matters for what it fed.

n: The Pilgrim Road from Siloam to the Temple
pl: City of David and the Temple Mount
w: A stepped, paved street about 600 m long ran from the Pool of Siloam up toward the Temple, with shops and drains along the way. Coins found under its pavement suggest it was built about AD 30.
m: This is the street pilgrims took when they came for the festivals; Jesus and the Twelve would have walked it with the crowds.
c: The date comes from a limited number of coins and is not accepted by everyone.

pl: North of the Temple Mount, near the Sheep Gate
per: Hasmonean–Herodian pools; Roman healing shrine 2nd century AD
w: Two huge pools lay side by side, separated by a rock wall, with colonnades on all four sides and on the dividing wall, five porticoes in all. Later a Roman healing shrine (an Asklepieion) was built beside them.
m: John 5 begins with “a pool in Jerusalem, near the Sheep Gate, called Bethesda, which has five porticoes”. The discovery matches the detail, one of the Gospel’s most exact descriptions.
c: The healing shrine was added after Jesus’ time.

n: A scale model of Jerusalem in Jesus’ day
w: A 1:50 scale model of Jerusalem at its height just before AD 70, built from excavations and from the descriptions of Josephus, shows the walls, the Temple, Herod’s palace and the theater.
m: It is useful for seeing how the places in the Gospels fit together: the Temple, the Antonia, Herod’s palace, the pools and the garden east of the city.
c: It is a reconstruction. New digs keep changing details.

per: Pavement from about AD 135; traditional since the Middle Ages
w: Large paving stones, some scratched with gaming boards, lie under the Sisters of Zion convent. They were long said to be the courtyard where Pilate judged Jesus.
m: John 19:13 says Pilate sat “at a place called the Stone Pavement, and in Aramaic Gabbatha”. The pavement is among the sites visited on the Via Dolorosa.
c: Most archaeologists date this pavement to the time of Hadrian, a century after Jesus. John names a real place, but this particular pavement is a later work.

w: At the Citadel by the Jaffa Gate, the base of one of Herod’s three towers and parts of his palace walls survive. The palace stood in the city’s highest part and became the governor’s residence in Jerusalem.
m: Many scholars think Pilate judged Jesus at this palace, not at the Antonia fortress. Josephus and Philo say the governors stayed there when in Jerusalem.
c: The location of the trial is a scholarly argument: Herod’s palace or the Antonia fortress.

n: The Mount of Olives and the road from Bethphage
per: Cemetery in use from the First Temple period; churches from the 4th century
w: A long ridge east of the city, its slope covered by about 150,000 Jewish graves, some from Jesus’ own time. Chapels mark the Lord’s Prayer, the weeping over Jerusalem (Dominus Flevit, where first-century tombs were found) and the Ascension.
m: The road from Bethphage, over the summit and down into the Kidron Valley, is Jesus’ route on Palm Sunday. From here you look straight across to the Temple Mount, where he predicts its fall.
c: Individual chapels are traditional; the mountain itself is exactly as described.
r: Mark 11:1-11; Matthew 21:1-9; Luke 19:28-44; Mark 13:3; Matthew 24:3; Luke 22:39; John 12:12-19

pl: Foot of the Mount of Olives
per: Church of All Nations 1924, over a 4th-century church
w: The Aramaic name means “oil press”. A modern church stands over the rock honored as the place of Jesus’ prayer, and ancient olive trees in the garden are among the oldest in the region. A nearby cave with an olive press and cisterns is also venerated.
m: All four Gospels set Jesus’ arrest in an olive garden across the Kidron, just east of the city. The name fits both the trees and the oil presses that processed their harvest.
c: Studies date the oldest trees to about 900 years, and Rome cut down the trees around Jerusalem in AD 70.

n: The Cenacle: the traditional Upper Room
per: Crusader hall (about 12th–14th century) over a 4th-century church
w: A Gothic hall on Mount Zion, built by the Crusaders over earlier churches that go back to the 4th century. Below it is a shrine long venerated as the tomb of David.
m: Mount Zion has been remembered as the place of the Last Supper and Pentecost since the early church. The Gospels say only that Jesus sent two disciples to prepare “a large upper room, furnished and ready”.
c: The room you visit is medieval. A first-century upper room could have stood near here, but no evidence confirms it.

n: The tombs of the Kidron Valley
w: Along the valley between the city and the Mount of Olives stand monumental rock-cut tombs with names such as Absalom’s Pillar, the Tomb of Zechariah and the Tomb of Bnei Hezir, the last carrying an inscription naming priests of the Hezir family.
m: Jesus denounces scribes who “build the tombs of the prophets and decorate the graves of the righteous.” These tombs are exactly that kind of memorial, and Jesus crossed this valley to Gethsemane.
c: The traditional names (Absalom, Zechariah) are later labels; they are not the original owners.

w: The steep Hinnom Valley wraps around the south of the old city. On its far slope are many first-century rock tombs and the Greek Orthodox Monastery of St. Onuphrius, built on the traditional “Field of Blood”.
m: Jesus uses the Hinnom Valley (Gehenna) as an image of judgement. Matthew says the chief priests bought a potter’s field with Judas’s returned silver and called it the Field of Blood.
c: The spot is traditional. Gehenna is an image drawn from the valley’s history.
r: Matthew 27:3-10; Matthew 5:22; Matthew 5:29-30; Matthew 10:28; Mark 9:43-48; Luke 12:5

n: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre
per: First-century quarry and tombs; church begun about AD 326
w: Constantine’s builders cut away a hillside to expose a tomb identified by the local Christian community, and built a church around it. Under the church are first-century burial caves, and the 2016 renovation of the shrine briefly exposed the original rock bench of the tomb.
m: John says Jesus was crucified “near the city”, in a garden with a new tomb. This site was a quarry outside the city wall in Jesus’ day, later turned into tombs, which matches the Gospel details.
c: Many scholars find it plausible, but there is no inscription naming the tomb. The case rests on early local memory.
r: John 19:17-20; John 19:41-42; Mark 15:22; Mark 15:46; Matthew 27:33; Luke 23:33; Luke 23:53; Matthew 28:1-8; Mark 16:1-8

per: Tomb cut in the Iron Age (about 8th–7th century BC); identification from 1883
w: A peaceful garden with a rock-cut tomb north of the Old City. It was popularized as Jesus’ tomb in the 19th century and remains a place of prayer for many Protestants.
m: It offers a picture of what a garden tomb looked like, with a rock-cut chamber, a low entrance and a long groove in front (its original purpose is debated).
c: Most archaeologists date the tomb to the Old Testament period, so it cannot be Jesus’ tomb.

n: Rolling-stone tombs of the Herodian period
w: Some wealthy tombs around Jerusalem, among them Herod’s Family Tomb and the Tomb of the Kings, were sealed with a great round stone that rolled in a groove across the entrance. Most burial caves were closed with a square block.
m: The Gospels say a great stone was rolled to close Jesus’ tomb and rolled away at Easter. These tombs show what that looked like and that such a tomb belonged to someone of means (Joseph of Arimathea was rich).
c: The Gospels say “rolled”, but don’t describe a disc; a square stone can also be rolled.
r: Matthew 27:60; Mark 15:46; Mark 16:3-4; Luke 24:2; John 11:38-39; John 20:1; Matthew 28:2

w: For about a century before AD 70, Jerusalem families collected a loved one’s bones after the flesh had decayed and put them in small limestone boxes, often scratched with names. Hundreds are known, with names such as Mary, Joseph, Simon, Jesus and Lazarus.
m: It shows how ordinary the Gospel names were. Jesus’ burial in a tomb, and the Gospels’ concern about uncleanness from graves, make more sense against this background.
c: An ossuary reading “Jesus son of Joseph” is real but means little: both names were common.
r: John 11:17; John 11:38-44; Matthew 23:27-29; Luke 11:44; Matthew 8:21-22; Matthew 1:16; Matthew 1:18-25; Luke 7:11-15

n: The crucified man of Giv’at ha-Mivtar
w: A heel bone from an ossuary in a Jerusalem tomb was pierced by an 11.5 cm iron nail, with traces of olive wood still attached. The ossuary was inscribed “Yehohanan”. It is the only skeletal remains of a crucified man known from Roman Judea.
m: It shows that crucifixion in Judea involved nails, as in John’s account of the marks on Jesus’ hands and feet, and that the victim could be buried by his family in a family tomb.
c: Original claims about how he was positioned were revised in 1985. Its date and the nail’s role are still debated.

per: Church from about AD 380; well deep in antiquity
w: A deep well inside a Greek Orthodox church marks the traditional spot, honored since at least the 4th century. It is fed by groundwater and was once about 40 m (130 ft) deep. A church was built here around AD 380 and rebuilt several times.
m: John says the woman was surprised that Jesus, with no bucket, could draw water: “the well is deep.” The site is also in the heart of Samaritan country, between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal.
c: This is one of the few Gospel sites with a continuous, undisputed tradition.

per: Temple precinct built about 200 BC; destroyed about 111 BC
w: Excavators found a large sacred precinct on the summit with a temple platform, altars and hundreds of inscriptions in Aramaic and Hebrew. John Hyrcanus destroyed it about 111 BC. The Samaritans still make Passover offerings on the mountain.
m: The Samaritan woman asks Jesus whether people should worship on “this mountain” or in Jerusalem. The hostility behind that question was centuries old.

w: Herod rebuilt the old city of Samaria as Sebaste, honoring Augustus, with a temple, a forum, a stadium, a colonnaded street and strong walls. Its Roman ruins still stand on a hilltop.
m: Jesus travelled “between Samaria and Galilee,” and Samaria was home to the people he made the heroes of two stories. The Gospels never name this city.
c: It shows Samaria’s Roman-era setting; no Gospel event happens here.

w: A large Greek-style city below a mound, with a well-preserved Roman theater, a colonnaded street, bathhouses and a hippodrome. It was the only Decapolis city west of the Jordan.
m: The Gospels say crowds from the Decapolis followed Jesus, and the healed man proclaimed his story across the region. These cities were Greek in culture, showing a different world from the Jewish villages of Galilee.
c: Gospel texts do not mention Scythopolis by name.

per: Roman city; excavated colonnades from the 2nd–4th century
w: The Roman city at Tyre has a vast hippodrome, a long colonnaded road and large cemeteries. It was a great Phoenician port long before and after Jesus.
m: Jesus withdraws to the district of Tyre and Sidon and meets a Gentile woman whose faith he praises. He also remarks that Tyre and Sidon would have repented had they seen the signs he did in Galilee.
c: Most of what is visible is later than Jesus.
r: Matthew 15:21-28; Mark 7:24-30; Matthew 11:21-22; Luke 6:17; Luke 10:13-14; Mark 3:7-8

per: Roman and Byzantine remains at several sites
w: Emmaus-Nicopolis (Imwas) has a Roman city and Byzantine church, Abu Ghosh a Crusader church, Qubeibeh a Franciscan shrine over a Roman villa. Another candidate, Motza, is only about 6 km from Jerusalem.
m: Luke says Emmaus was “about seven miles from Jerusalem” (60 stadia), though some early manuscripts say 160 stadia. The village’s identity is unsettled.
c: Nobody knows which Emmaus it was.

w: Two tiny rolled silver amulets, found in a burial cave, carry the priestly blessing “The Lord bless you and keep you” in ancient Hebrew script. They are the oldest known fragments of any biblical text.
m: The blessing is the one priests spoke over the people. In Luke, Zechariah is a priest, and the risen Jesus lifts his hands in blessing as he leaves.
c: They are from the First Temple period, long before the Gospels.

w: Excavations at the mounds of Kuyunjik and Nebi Yunus uncovered the palaces of the Assyrian kings and the library of Ashurbanipal, with tens of thousands of clay tablets. Parts were badly damaged in 2014–17.
m: Jesus says the people of Nineveh will stand up at the judgement because they repented at Jonah’s preaching, and “something greater than Jonah is here”.

n: Papyri, contracts and phylacteries from the Judean desert
w: Dry caves have preserved legal papyri: marriage contracts, land deeds and certificates of divorce, along with tiny leather phylactery boxes holding Scripture, used for prayer.
m: They show how often marriage and divorce were a legal matter, which sheds light on the Pharisees’ question about divorce. Phylacteries and tassels explain Jesus’ remark about people who make theirs wide.
r: Matthew 19:3-9; Mark 10:2-12; Matthew 23:5; Matthew 5:31; Matthew 1:18-25; Luke 16:6-7

n: Stone vessels: cups and jars that stay clean
w: Cups, mugs and large jars were turned or carved from soft chalkstone, which Jewish law considered immune to ritual impurity. They appear in huge numbers in Jerusalem, Galilee and Judea in Jesus’ time. The big jars hold roughly 80–120 liters.
m: John mentions six stone water jars used for purification at the wedding in Cana. They are right for the setting and for the amount of wine Jesus made.

w: Hundreds of stepped, plastered pools have been found in Jerusalem, Qumran, Sepphoris, Magdala and Gamla, with private ones in rich houses and public ones near the Temple. Most have a divided stairway, one side for going down, one for coming up.
m: They were used to become ritually clean. They explain the washings the Gospels mention, the question about hand-washing and the baptism of John.
r: John 2:6; John 3:25; Mark 7:3-4; Luke 11:38; John 13:10; Mark 1:4-5

w: Small, hand-sized clay lamps, with a round body and a pinched spout (the “Herodian lamp”), are among the most common finds. A lamp burned a little olive oil for an hour or two.
m: Jesus’ images of lamps are everyday ones: lamps are put on a stand, kept filled while waiting for the bridegroom, and used to see the room.
r: Matthew 5:15; Matthew 25:1-13; Luke 8:16; Luke 11:33-36; Luke 12:35; Matthew 6:22-23; Mark 4:21; John 3:19-21; John 5:35; John 8:12

n: Wine and oil presses, vineyards and terraces
w: Rock-cut treading floors with collecting vats, watchtowers and stone terraces survive across the hills of Judea and Galilee, along with stone olive-crushing basins and beam presses.
m: Vineyards and olive groves were common, so Jesus’ parable of the tenants builds a wall, a winepress and a tower for the vineyard, as every listener would have known.
r: Mark 12:1; Matthew 21:33; Matthew 7:16; Luke 6:44; Luke 5:37-39; John 15:1-5; Luke 16:6; Matthew 20:1-16; Luke 14:28-30; Luke 20:9-19

w: Smooth, rock-cut circles on hilltops were used to thresh and winnow grain, and rock-cut pits and stone-lined silos stored it.
m: John the Baptist’s picture of wheat gathered into the barn while the chaff burns, the parable of the weeds, and the rich man’s plan to build bigger barns all use these familiar scenes.
r: Matthew 3:12; Luke 3:17; Matthew 13:24-30; Luke 12:16-21; Matthew 6:26; Matthew 12:1-8; Mark 4:3-8; Mark 4:26-29

w: Heavy basalt rotary querns, turned by hand or hourglass mills turned by donkeys, are common finds. A great millstone weighed as much as a person could carry.
m: Jesus’ warning about anyone who causes a child to stumble, that it would be better to have a great millstone hung around the neck, and his picture of two women grinding at the mill, use daily household tools.

w: Galilean homes were small basalt or fieldstone rooms around a shared courtyard, with flat roofs of beams, branches and packed clay, reached by an outside stair. In Jerusalem’s Upper City, wealthy homes had mosaics, dining rooms and private baths.
m: A paralyzed man’s friends can tear through a roof, a woman can sweep her house for a lost coin, and a wise builder digs down to rock, because Jesus’ audience lived in houses like these.
r: Mark 2:1-12; Luke 5:17-26; Matthew 7:24-27; Luke 15:8-10; Luke 14:15-24; Matthew 6:6; Matthew 22:1-14; Luke 7:36-50; John 14:2

w: Rome paved and marked key routes, with milestones, and Herod’s sons collected tolls where roads crossed borders. Capernaum lay on the road between Antipas’s Galilee and Philip’s territory.
m: This is the world of Levi (Matthew) sitting at his toll booth, of Zacchaeus the chief tax collector, and of the soldier who could make you carry his pack one mile.
c: Customs stations are described in writing; none from the Gospel period has been excavated at Capernaum.

w: Wealthy houses in Jerusalem’s Upper City had dining rooms with frescoed walls, mosaic floors, private ritual baths and imported tableware. Jewish custom at Passover was to recline on couches around the table. Josephus says the priests counted over 250,000 lambs offered one year.
m: John 13–17 is set around the Last Supper, and John says one disciple was “reclining next to Jesus”. The farewell conversations in John 14–17 take place within this meal setting.
c: The Gospels do not say whose house it was or where. This shows only what a dining room of the time looked like.
